rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan sūra is conventionally thirty-fifth in revelation order and followed Sūrat Qāf.
rows.anchor: السورة مكية، ترتيبها الخامسة والثلاثون على المشهور في ترتيب النزول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Balad and al-Qiyāma are the only sūras opening with an explicit oath preceded by lā; the same formula appears elsewhere within Meccan sūras.
rows.anchor: وهي إحدى سورتين ابتدأتا بلفظ القسم صريحاً مسبوقاً بـ: لا والسورة الأخرى هي القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across these occurrences, God is the speaker of the oath.
rows.anchor: وفعل القسم فيها جميعاً، مسند إلى الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: جمهرة المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes gloss lā uqsim as ‘I swear,’ treating lā as added emphasis without explaining the rhetorical shift or how negation reinforces an oath.
rows.anchor: وجمهرة المفسرين يكتفون هنا بالقول

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: He explains lā uqsim as an Arab oath formula that reinforces a manifest report needing no oath, or magnifies an object too great to require magnification by oath.
rows.anchor: كأن القائل يقول: إني لا أعظمه بالقسم

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He reports a literal negation: God does not swear by this city because its people have acted in ways that warrant violation of its sanctity.
rows.anchor: أن هذا البلد لا يقسم الله به وقد جاء أهله بأعمال توجب إحلال حرمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic usage confines lā uqsim to divine speech and never presents God’s oath without lā; denying any need for an oath therefore confirms the assertion.
rows.anchor: إلا حين يكون الفعل مسنداً إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author compares the construction with ordinary phrases such as ‘I need not recommend him’ or ‘without an oath,’ which affirm trust and certainty.
rows.anchor: ومن مألوف استعمالنا أن نقول: لا أوصيك بفلان، تأكيداً للتوصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Arabic usage does not bar substituting aqsama with ahlafa, the author cites oath verses by al-Nābigha, al-Aʿshā, and Shās ibn ʿAbda; Qur’anic usage will complicate this apparent equivalence.
rows.anchor: فقد يبدو من السهل هنا أن نفسر أقسم بلفظ أحلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses the root ḥ-l-f thirteen times, always in contexts of breaking or abusing oaths, including hypocrites exposed after Tabūk.
rows.anchor: في القرآن الكريم في ثلاثة عشر موضعاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other hypocrite passages likewise associate ḥ-l-f with known falsehood and lying oaths.
rows.anchor: ومعها، في المنافقين أيضاً، آيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author includes al-Qalam’s condemnation of a contemptible habitual oath-taker among the negative uses of this root.
rows.anchor: ولا تطع كل حلاف مهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Six cited verses in al-Tawba expose hypocrites whose oaths conceal lies after Tabūk.
rows.anchor: منها ست آيات في المنافقين الذين فضحتهم سورة التوبة بعد غزوة تبوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath root is used in the hypocrites’ false excuse in al-Nisāʾ, while believers’ oath-breaking is tied to expiation; qasam instead conveys a solemn or sincerely held assertion.
rows.anchor: وجاء الفعل مرة واحدة مسنداً إلى الذين آمنوا، فلزمتهم كفارة الحنث باليمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although dictionaries may call the words synonyms, Qur’anic patterns and the close relation of ḥalafa to ḥinth indicate a fine semantic distinction from qasam.
rows.anchor: وصنيع القرآن فيهما يلفت إلى فرق دقيق بين اللفظين المقول بترادفهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree that ‘this city’ in the oath is Mecca.
rows.anchor: المقسم به في الآية، هو "مكة"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qur’anic usage, the definite singular al-balad paired with ‘this’ identifies Mecca, as in al-Balad, al-Tīn, and Abraham’s prayer.
rows.anchor: مشاراً إليه بهذا، فإن الإشارة تعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without the demonstrative, al-balad can mean any wholesome town rather than Mecca specifically.
rows.anchor: وجاء البلد، بغير اسم الإشارة، في آية الأعراف 58 وليست خاصة بمكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite singular balad can denote Mecca in Abraham’s prayer, while other indefinite examples mean a town generically.
rows.anchor: أما بلد، بالإفراد والتنكير، فقد جاء مرة في دعاء إبراهيم لمكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Abu Ḥayyān’s literal-negation reading: divine lā can deny the need for an oath while affirming the city’s sanctity and deploring inherited abuses by its people.
rows.anchor: ويبقى القسم في الآية على وجهه من تعظيم حرمة هذا البلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 2 is syntactically and lexically connected to the oath: the circumstantial wāw qualifies verse 1, and the repeated demonstrative reinforces their link.
rows.anchor: من ناحيتين: واو الحال، وهي قيد للجملة الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes ḥill as the Meccans treating the Prophet’s protected person as lawful to harm in a sanctuary where even animals and offenders were safe.
rows.anchor: هو من استحلال حرمة الرسول في البلد الحرام الذي يأمن فيه الطير والوحش والجاني

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: To address the apparent conflict between the city’s sanctity and its people’s persecution of the Prophet, he takes lā as negating the oath.
rows.anchor: قال "أبو حيان" في (البحر) إن "لا" نافية للقسم

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: He explains the Prophet’s being ḥill as the Meccans allowing themselves to persecute and drive him out, despite the city’s divinely granted security and honor.
rows.anchor: وقال الشيخ محمد عبده: "ومعنى كونه حلا، أنه استحل لأهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view reads ḥill as God’s future permission for the Prophet to capture or kill in Mecca after its conquest.
rows.anchor: فأنت حل به في المستقبل، تصنع فيه ما تريد من القتل والأسر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: To explain the pre-conquest revelation, he says the future is presented as if already witnessed, comparing it with the announcement of death in 39:30.
rows.anchor: فقال الزمخشري يجيب عن سؤال طرحه في هذا الموقف

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He rejects the future-license interpretation as an unnecessary grammatical problem and instead reads ḥill as the Prophet’s residence in Mecca at revelation.
rows.anchor: وأما سؤاله والجواب، فهذا لا يسأله من له أدنى تعلق بالنحو

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: He also proposes ḥill as the opposite of iḥrām, meaning release from consecration.
rows.anchor: ذكره إبتن القيم في التبيان

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: He and Ibn al-Qayyim offer a fourth sense: ḥill means residence, opposite of departure.
rows.anchor: وقول رابع: أنه من الحلول بمعنى الإقامة ضد الظعن، ذكره الراغب

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He says the oath honors both Mecca’s attachment to God and the Prophet’s presence and residence there.
rows.anchor: أقسم بها لما جمعت من الشرفين: شرفها بإضافتها إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root ḥ-l-l spans residence, release from consecration, violation of sanctity, and perhaps its original image of untying a knot; the author links the latter to Moses’ prayer.
rows.anchor: وربما كان آصل معنى فيه، حل العقدة، ومنه دعاء موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root also developed the religious contrast of lawful versus forbidden and iḥlāl versus iḥrām; most Qur’anic occurrences of ḥill mean lawful.
rows.anchor: ثم نقلت إلى المصطلح الديني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers Abu Ḥayyān’s reading of ḥill as residence; it fits the context while carrying an echo of the Meccans violating the Prophet’s sanctity.
rows.anchor: ونطمئن إلى تفسير آية البلد بالحلول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly called Mecca the land dearest to God and to him when emigrating.
rows.anchor: لأحب أرض الله إلى الله وأحب أرض الله إلى رسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds ‘release from consecration’ poorly suited to the context and rejects future divine license after the conquest as strained and linguistically unsupported.
rows.anchor: كما نستبعد أن يكون حل بمعنى إحلال الله لرسوله هذا البلد يفعل به بعد الفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading ḥill as residence, with an echo of persecution, joins the verses naturally; the author prefers a circumstantial clause over the parenthetical reading of al-Zamakhsharī and Muḥammad ʿAbduh.
rows.anchor: تفسير الحل بالإقامة وهو المعنى المتبادر، أو يجعل أذى الرسول حلالا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He, followed by Muḥammad ʿAbduh, treats verse 2 as parenthetical and says it stresses Mecca’s great rank in every circumstance.
rows.anchor: قاله "الزمخشري" وتابعه على ذلك الشيخ محمد عبده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The circumstantial reading binds the first oath to verse 3: ‘a parent and what he begot’ is coordinated with the city, whose inhabitants’ conditions the Prophet experiences.
rows.anchor: معطوفان على هذا البلد في الآية الأولى

rows.speaker: جمهرة المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes take mā as a relative pronoun, then differ over the phrase’s referent.
rows.anchor: على أن جمهرة المفسرين، ذهبوا إلى أن "ما" هنا اسم موصول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Most exegetes take mā as a relative pronoun; al-Zamakhsharī says the indefinite wording creates an open-ended effect of praise and wonder.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: هو للإبهام المستقل بالمدح والتعجب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported by al-Ṭabarī and Abu Ḥayyān to understand parent and offspring as all animals.
rows.anchor: أطلقه قوم، منهم إبن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن جرير الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī’s broad interpretation includes humans, animals, and plants; Muḥammad ʿAbduh adopts it as well.
rows.anchor: ومنهم إبن جرير الطبري، عاماً في البشر والحيوان والنبات

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Zamakhsharī are cited for identifying the parent and offspring as Adam and all his descendants.
rows.anchor: ذوريته "إبن القيم، وذكره الزمخشري"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other exegetes narrow the referent to righteous descendants.
rows.anchor: وخصه قوم: بالصالحين من ذريته

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A reported possibility restricts the phrase to Muḥammad and his community; al-Ṭabarī gives it tentatively, al-Zamakhsharī cites it, and Abu Ḥayyān attributes it to Mujāhid.
rows.anchor: ذكره أبو حيان مروياً عن "مجاهد"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed referents are Noah and his descendants, or Abraham and all his offspring.
rows.anchor: وفي قول: إنه نوح وذريته، أو إبراهيم عليه السلام وجميع ولده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author doubts that all proposed referents fit the Arabic and argues none explains the phrase’s rhetorical relation to the city in the oath.
rows.anchor: إن آدم مرجع العباد، كما أن مكة مرجع البلاد

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Those identifying Adam and his descendants justify the honor by making Adam the source of humankind as Mecca is the destination of lands.
rows.anchor: بعد ما أقسم ببلده، مبالغة في شرفه - صلى الله عليه وسلم - (الطبير

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Those identifying Muḥammad and his community say the oath honors them after the oath by his city; Abu Ḥayyān transmits this explanation.
rows.anchor: قالوا إن القسم هنا لتعظيم الله محمداً وأمته، بعد ما أقسم ببلده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universal reading sees reproduction across plants, animals, and people as a remarkable stage of existence and a display of wisdom and craftsmanship.
rows.anchor: ليلفت نظرنا إلى رفعة هذا الطور من أطوار الوجود، وهو طور التوالد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the long account of reproduction in nature is unsupported by the verse and disconnected from the city to which the phrase is coordinated.
rows.anchor: وما أرى نص الآية، يحتمل كل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may concern the powerful Abu al-Ashadd, who challenged others to pull him from a hide, or al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, notorious for pride in his status and wealth; the author says the wording generalizes beyond any possibly authentic occasion.
rows.anchor: هو من قول: أبو الأشد، كان قوياً

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He takes the target as humanity generally: people become tyrannical when they think themselves self-sufficient, then deluded by strength and wealth.
rows.anchor: كما فهم "أبو حيان" وإن الإنسان ليطغى أن رآه استغنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubad occurs only here in the Qur’an and means a dense, accumulated multitude, from wool felted together; the word can describe a lion’s thick mane or dense foliage.
rows.anchor: لم يأت في القرآن في غير هذا الموضع، وهو في اللغة الكثير المجتمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘I destroyed/spent’ rather than ‘I spent’ better suits the speaker’s vanity, arrogance, boasting, and self-display.
rows.anchor: يقول: أهلكت، ولم يقل: أنفقت، مع قربها، إذ الإهلاك أولى بالغرور والطغيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite ‘wealth,’ ‘abundant,’ and ‘anyone’ are deliberately unrestricted and general.
rows.anchor: مقصود به إلى الإطلاق والتعميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second rebuking question shifts from lan about future power to lam about past surveillance: the arrogant person’s entire past is already encompassed, after God’s control of his destiny was established.
rows.anchor: التي تنصرف إلى الماضي فتقرر أن ماضي المغتر محسوب عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eyes, tongue, and lips signify accountable use of sight and speech, not merely body parts shared with animals; this prepares the warning about moral responsibility and the consequences of words.
rows.anchor: وإنما يراد بها ما يسأل الإنسان عنه، على وجه الحض والزجر بالحجة، من أمانة البصر والنطق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hudā originally evokes a protruding stone that keeps a traveler from stumbling, daylight that reveals the road, then a caravan’s leading camel and guide; it came to mean guidance rather than error and, religiously, inspiration or enabling grace.
rows.anchor: في الهداية ضد الضلال، وهو أكثر المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najd means elevated ground or a clear uphill road; related forms describe tall, forward-moving camels and came to suggest a visible guide leading a people.
rows.anchor: والنجد لغة: ما أشرف من الأرض، والطريق المرافع الواضح

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib interprets the two paths as truth and falsehood in belief, truth and lies in speech, and good and bad in action.
rows.anchor: وفسر "الراغب" النجدين في الآية، بطريق الحق والباطل

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority, including al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn al-Qayyim, and Muḥammad ʿAbduh, take the two heights as the paths of good and evil.
rows.anchor: وذكر "أبو حيان" أن هذا هو ما عليه الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A view in al-Asās, al-Baḥr, and al-Muḥīṭ identifies the two paths as breasts nourishing a child; the author considers this strained and weak.
rows.anchor: والتأويل به، فيه شطط التكلف مع ظهور وهنه وضعفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We guided him’ implies God inspired innate human discrimination of good and evil and supplied sensory means; the unique Qur’anic word najdayn highlights the paths’ visible clarity.
rows.anchor: الهدى ملحوظ فيه أنه تعالى ألهم الفطرة الإنسانية الإدراك المميز للخير والشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence shows a human equipped with senses and innate discernment to bear the difficult trust of moral responsibility and choose between the clearly visible paths.
rows.anchor: فهذا الإنسان الذي خلقه الله مهيأ لأمانة التكليف الصعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past tense with alam suits senses granted before the arrogant person feels powerful, while lan projects forward his deluded claim that no one will ever overpower him.
rows.anchor: أما حسبانه أن لن يقدر عليه أحد، فيأتي متأخراً بعد أن تطغيه القوة والمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past and future references show that God governs the human being’s entire course, from creation to final return; the discussion invokes the opening revelation’s warning about human arrogance.
rows.anchor: بيان لمدى إحاطة الله بالإنسان مهما يبلغ من قوته وطغيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God owns human destiny across past and future: He is the creator, and to Him is the return, as stated in the first revealed sūra.
rows.anchor: ما يملك من حاضره وماضيه

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines iqtihām as entering into frightening hardship; its Qur’anic root occurs only here and at Ṣād 38:59.
rows.anchor: الأقتحام: توسط شدة مخيفة، فيما فسره "الراغب"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root’s older senses include a road’s rugged passages, the hard final three nights of a lunar month, and crossing deserts; ʿaqaba is a difficult mountain ascent.
rows.anchor: وأصل القحمة، من الطريق: مصاعبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtihām aptly pairs with ʿaqaba because both convey hardship and endurance; the image suits humans created in toil and equipped to face arduous moral choices.
rows.anchor: والاقتحام هو أنسب الألفاظ للعقبة لما بينهما من تلاؤم في الشدة والمجاهدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes take lā as negative but leave the prefixed fa unexplained; their grammatical difficulty is that ordinary negative lā does not independently govern a past verb, as al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj say through Abu Ḥayyān.
rows.anchor: وقد ساق "أبو حيان" قول الفراء والزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right side evokes strength, goodness and optimism, receiving one’s record in the right hand, the saved, and also the sanctity of an oath and religious faith.
rows.anchor: وملحظ الخير والتفاؤل في إيتاء المؤمن كتابه بيمينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s contrast implies that disbelief in God’s signs opposes the steep path of freeing a slave, feeding in famine, faith, and mutual counsel to patience and compassion; shu’m is the opposite of yumn.
rows.anchor: فدل ذلك من صنيع القرآن على أن الكفر بآيات الله، مقابل لاقتحام العقبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muʾṣada means tightly sealed with no exit; the author traces it to waṣīd, an enclosure among mountain stones, while al-Zamakhsharī derives it from closing a door.
rows.anchor: ونرى أن الإيصاد ليس مجرد الإغلاق، وإنما فيه الشدة والإحكام الملحوظان في أصل المادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saved people on Resurrection day are called the companions of the right hand and the companions of the right side.
rows.anchor: وأهل الجنة يوم القيامة: هم أصحاب اليمين، وأصحاب الميمنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic cognate al-waṣīd appears in the cave narrative as the place where the Companions’ dog rests.
rows.anchor: الوصيد في آية الكهف 18

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Humaza’s parallel use of muʾṣada, in a Meccan sūra revealed after al-Qiyāma, reinforces the account of an interdependent, merciful community and the Qur’an’s condemnation of greed and selfishness.
rows.anchor: والاستئناس بها هنا يزيدنا تمثلاً للمجتمع الإسلامي المتعاون المتكافل المتراحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author agrees with al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, and Abu Ḥayyān that the repetition intensifies a warning; the sūra’s tone is consistently threatening.
rows.anchor: وتأكيد للوعيد والنذير، وهو ما اطمأن إليه الطبري والزمخشري وأبو حيان

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported as taking the first warning for disbelievers and the second as a promise to believers; the author rejects this split in tone.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك: أن الآية الأولى للكفار فهي وعيد، وان الثانية للمؤمنين فهي وعد

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report attributed to ʿAlī assigns the first warning to the grave and the second to resurrection; al-Naysābūrī also gives this view.
rows.anchor: وأخرى عن "علي" كرم الله وجهه

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī lists four readings: emphasis; disbelievers threatened then believers promised; the first at death and second in grave questioning; or grave punishment followed by resurrection punishment.
rows.anchor: وأورد "الرازي" أربعة وجوه في التكرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects interpretations that make parallel clauses carry opposite threat and promise, or assign them separate times merely to preserve a temporal sense of thumma.
rows.anchor: وليس النص القرآني في وضوح بيانه بمسئول عن هذا الخلاف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says thumma here is not temporal; it intensifies the warning, as in repeatedly telling someone not to do something.
rows.anchor: ونقول هنا ما قاله الومخشري، إن ثم في هذا السياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both clauses address those distracted by accumulation; repetition intensifies their rebuke and warning rather than dividing the audience.
rows.anchor: إلا للذين ألهلهم التكاثر، ما التكرير إلا مبالغة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines knowledge as grasping a thing in its reality; the author distinguishes this clear, assured knowing from mere recognition.
rows.anchor: والعلم إدراك الشيء بحقيقته كعبارة "الراغب" في مفرداته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lexical family of ʿilm is associated with visible marks and signs, then with knowledge that clearly discloses a thing’s reality.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا الوضوح المميو في العلامة والعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an calls God ʿālim and ʿalīm, never ʿārif; divine knowledge encompasses hidden matters, secrets, hearts, and all creation.
rows.anchor: نرى الله تعالى يوصف بالعالم ولا يوصف بالعارف، والعليم من أسمائه الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For humans, knowledge is acquired certainty or forewarning of an undeniable day; sawfa taʿlamūn elsewhere warns that truth will be disclosed.
rows.anchor: وحين يسند العلم إلى البشر فهو العلم الكسبي عندما يكون على وجه التأكد واليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those absorbed in accumulation will discover its reality when graves swallow what they amassed and the veil is lifted, as in Qāf.
rows.anchor: فناسب هذا الإلهاء أن ينذرهم بما بعده من تلقف المقابر لكل ما يتكاثرون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verses specify what they will learn, so the author sees no need to ask the question debated by al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, and al-Rāzī.
rows.anchor: ولا حاجة بنا إلى الوقوف لنسأل عما سوف يعلمونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge of certainty leaves no room for doubt or heedlessness, and the following declaration that they will see Hell clarifies it.
rows.anchor: هو علم اليقين، حين لا مجال لشك فيه أو ارتياب

rows.speaker: جمهرة المفسرين
rows.claim: The author defines Qur’anic certainty as verified perception that expels doubt, a sense sustained across the different forms of the word.
rows.anchor: اليقين في القرآن التحقق وإزاحة الشك، والإدراك الواثق

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Qur’anic examples place certainty opposite doubt and supposition, and describe knowledge as settled and verified.
rows.anchor: مما لايدع مجالاً لتفسير اليقين بغير التحقق والإدراك الواثق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects identifying certainty here, or in 15:99, with death or resurrection; the phrase denotes verified perception that expels doubt, as Qur’anic usage shows.
rows.anchor: تفسير اليقين هنا، ولا في آية الحجر التي نظروا بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next statements explain certainty as seeing Hell with the eye of certainty; ʿayn adds sensory force and intensifies the meaning.
rows.anchor: فهذا بيان لما سوف يعلمون يقيناً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that eye-language can express what brings comfort and satisfaction, illustrating the point with Moses’ mother and the prayer for pleasing spouses and children.
rows.anchor: كما استعمل ما يقر العين، فيما هو للإنسان موضع غبطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In expressions such as ‘I saw it with my own eye,’ eye signifies actual, certain perception rather than illusion or metaphor.
rows.anchor: فأنت تقول: لقيته عياناً، أي معاينة لا شك فيها، ورأيته رأى العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three verses form one clear sequence: they will know with certainty when they see Hell as certainty; the Qur’anic order does not warrant separating verse 5 from verse 6.
rows.anchor: والنسق القرآني لا يسمح بأن نفصل بين هذه الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators separate the conditional from its answer, although each clause then needs an unstated completion; they supply an implied consequence for verse 5 and a hidden oath for verse 6.
rows.anchor: راحوا يتأولون في الموضعين كليهما، ويتكلفون تتمة مفترضة لكل من الآيتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their objection is the grammatical maxim that law makes both condition and consequence impossible: connecting ‘you would see Hell’ would seem to deny the certain sight.
rows.anchor: أن "لو" حرف امتناع لامتناع

rows.speaker: النيسابوري
rows.claim: Al-Naysābūrī says the answer to law must be omitted because the question about blessings is certain; if seeing Hell were its answer, that sight would seem uncertain.
rows.anchor: قال النيسابورى: "اتفقوا على أن جواب لو محذوف

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī likewise says seeing Hell cannot answer law because that would entail that the sight does not occur.
rows.anchor: وقال الرازي: "اتفقوا على أن جواب لو محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says grammatical formalism breaks a meaningful sequence; connecting the verses makes sight of Hell itself the certainty that fulfills the warning.
rows.anchor: وهكذا تتدخل الصنعة النحوية في نسق البيان الأعلى، وتقطع ما بين الآيتين

rows.speaker: ابن هشام
rows.claim: Ibn Hishām surveys five uses of law and rejects the common claim that it necessarily makes both the condition and its consequence impossible, citing counterexamples including God’s inexhaustible words.
rows.anchor: "لو" تأتي في العربية على خمسة أوجه، بينها إبن هشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other Qur’anic examples of law challenge the rigid impossibility rule; the author says conditional wording can make the consequence more forceful once its impediment disappears.
rows.anchor: وقد أرى أن هذا الأسلوب، أقوى من الجملة الخبرية، في تأكيد الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The linked reading means that they will certainly know when they see Hell with certainty; once their present ignorance is removed, the conditional consequence is realized without doubt.
rows.anchor: حين يرون الجحيم عينن اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning’s repeated certainty that they will know removes doubt about the condition of law; when they know with certainty, seeing Hell and being questioned follow with certainty.
rows.anchor: فلم يبق شك في أن جهلهم بعلم اليقين زائل لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final question about blessings brings the threat to its climax.
rows.anchor: فيبلغ الوعيد ذروته، ويصل به إلى غاية منتهاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes differ over whether God or angels ask, but the Qur’an deliberately leaves the asker unnamed to focus attention on the question itself.
rows.anchor: والقرآن سكت عن ذكر السائل، تركيزاً للإهتمام في السؤال نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say only disbelievers are questioned; al-Naysābūrī and Abu Ḥayyān include everyone, while al-Zamakhsharī leaves the audience unspecified but treats the blessing as addressed to humanity.
rows.anchor: وقالوا: إن السؤال يومئذ للكفار، وقيل: بل هو للبشر كافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes distinguish a gracious, honoring question for believers from a rebuke for disbelievers; the author rejects this mixed tone as detached from the sūra’s warning to those distracted by accumulation.
rows.anchor: فالمؤمن يسأل إكرام وتشريف، والكافر يسأل سؤال توبيخ وتقريع

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī answers the objection that judgment precedes seeing Hell by allowing sequence to be nonchronological, as faith can be mentioned after actions despite logically preceding them.
rows.anchor: أجاب الرازي: "المراد: ثم أخبركم أنكم تسألون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view places the question after entry into Hell and cites the keepers asking each group whether a warner came.
rows.anchor: ومنها: أن السؤال يكون إذا دخلوا النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says ‘that day’ explicitly fixes the question to the day they see Hell as certainty, settling disputes over its timing.
rows.anchor: وآية التكاثر فيما ترى تحدد وقت السؤال بيومئذ

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī counts nine interpretations of the blessing, ranging from sandals to the Prophet, with food, drink, housing, health, shade, leisure, safety, sleep, wellbeing, and balanced form among them.
rows.anchor: بلغ ما عده "الرازي" منها تسعة وجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who identify the blessing as the Prophet cite God’s favor in sending a messenger to believers.
rows.anchor: أن تأويل النعيم برسول الله، يؤيده عندهم قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who identify it as food and water cite the people of Hell asking the people of Paradise for water and provision.
rows.anchor: وفي تأويله بالماء والطعام، ذكروا آية الأعراف

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report attributed to Anas says that when a needy man asked whether any blessing was upon him, the Prophet named shade, sandals, and cool water.
rows.anchor: حديثاً عن "أنس" أنه "لما نزلت الآية قام محتاج فقال

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says that after he, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar ate bread and meat and drank fresh water at Abū al-Haytham’s home, this was among the blessings about which they would be asked.
rows.anchor: فقال النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام: قوموا بنا إلى منزل أبي الهيثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naʿīm can mean ease and contentment, wealth, a white hand, or a lush meadow, as well as faith, guidance, shade, health, and sleep.
rows.anchor: الخفض والدعة، والمال، واليد البيضاء والروضة الناعمة

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī limits the question to worldly blessings: what people did with them and how they acquired them.
rows.anchor: يميل إلى تخصيصه بنعيم الدنيا

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers the unrestricted totality of blessings, taking the definite article as comprehensive.
rows.anchor: واختار "الرزي" إطلاق اللفظ على جميع النعم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī restricts the warning to people who pursue pleasure, food, drink, and amusement, distinguishing those who use God’s gifts for learning, work, and gratitude.
rows.anchor: فأما من تمتع بنعمة الله وأرزاقه التي لم يخلقها إلا لعباده

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines naʿīm as abundant blessing.
rows.anchor: وقال "الراغب": والنعيم النعمة الكثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author turns to Qur’anic usage to adjudicate the disagreement: niʿma, anʿām, naʿmāʾ, and naʿīm each carry a consistent nuance; niʿma denotes worldly good or guidance bestowed by God.
rows.anchor: والقرآن استعمل النعمة، والأنعم، والنعماء، والنعيم بملحظ من الدلالة
